# Synchronization Strategy

Most flakiness this project sees traces back to timing, not logic (see item
3.2's server-timeout findings and item 3.3's resilience work). This skill is
the standard every generated action and verification follows, so
`stabilizer` isn't repeatedly hand-fixing the same category of problem.

## Default: trust Playwright's auto-waiting

Playwright's built-in actionability checks (visible, stable, enabled,
receives events) already wait before `click`, `fill`, `check`, etc. **Do
not** add a manual `waitForTimeout()`/`sleep()` before a normal action -
that's the single most common thing to strip out of a generated script
during stabilization, and it should not have been there to begin with.

## When an explicit wait is justified

- **A known-slow element.** Per the item 3.2 finding (some elements take
  2-3 minutes to render under load against a default ~60-120s timeout), use
  a **targeted** `locator.waitFor({ state: "visible", timeout: ... })` on
  that specific element, not a global timeout increase - a global increase
  hides slow-render regressions everywhere instead of surfacing them where
  they actually happen.
- **A navigation or full page load** - `page.waitForURL()` or
  `waitForLoadState("networkidle")` after an action that triggers
  navigation, rather than waiting on a specific element that happens to
  appear after the new page settles.
- **An async side effect with no visible loading indicator** - if the UI
  gives no signal that something is in flight (no spinner, no disabled
  button), wait on the *result* becoming true (`expect.poll` or
  `locator.waitFor` on the eventual state), never a fixed delay guessed to
  be "long enough."

## What never to do

- Never `page.waitForTimeout(n)` as a fix for a flaky step - it's a
  guess that either wastes time (n too large) or doesn't fix the real
  problem (n too small, intermittently).
- Never widen `expect.timeout` or the global test `timeout` in
  `playwright.config.ts` to make a specific flaky test pass - that's a
  synchronization-strategy violation masquerading as configuration; fix the
  specific wait.
- Never assume a retry (`test.retry`) fixes a synchronization problem - a
  retry that passes on attempt two without any code change is a
  `execution-stabilization` quarantine candidate, not evidence the
  synchronization was fine.

## Diagnosing a timing failure

When `stabilizer` sees a failure that looks timing-related (element not
found/not actionable, intermittent across runs, passes on manual re-run),
capture the evidence Playwright already gives you before guessing at a fix:
trace, video, and (per item 3.2) request/response timing on the relevant
API call. Compare against the time-of-day pattern already being tracked for
the server-timeout theory - a locally-reproducible timing issue and a
server-load timing issue need different fixes, and treating one as the
other wastes a stabilization cycle.

## When this needs to change

If `analyze-skills` shows `synchronization-strategy` corrections
clustering around one page, one component type (e.g. a specific dropdown
that's always slow), or one time-of-day window, that's a signal for a more
specific rule here - not a one-off wait bolted onto a single test. Log it,
and let `skill-curator` fold the pattern back into this skill.

## Learned patterns

Read [references/learned-patterns.md](./references/learned-patterns.md) when writing a wait or diagnosing a timing failure. It holds waits engineers put in by hand: sleeps replaced by conditions, response and URL waits - fixes that recurred across several files and engineers and were approved by a reviewer (generated by `npm run learn-publish`; do not edit it by hand). Treat it as part of this skill.

If you hit a problem it does not cover, run `npm run lookup-fix -- "<problem>"`. After you fix it by hand, record the fix with `npm run learn-capture -- --worktree --write --why "<what was wrong>"` so it can become a pattern (see the **fix-knowledge-base** skill).
